On the asymptotic behaviour of the quantiles in the gamma distribution

Henrik Laurberg Pedersen
Abstract

The asymptotic behaviour of the quantiles in the gamma distribution are investigated as the shape parameter tends to zero. Some remarks about the behaviour at infinity are given.

Keywords: Gamma distribution, quantile, incomplete gamma function, asymptotic expansion.

2020 MSC: Primary 41A60; Secondary 33B20.

1 Introduction

The pp-quantile mp​(x)m_{p}(x) in the gamma distribution of shape parameter xx and scale parameter 11 is, for p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), given implicitly as

∫0mp​(x)e−t​tx−1​𝑑t=p​Γ​(x).\int_{0}^{m_{p}(x)}e^{-t}t^{x-1}\,dt=p\Gamma(x). (1)

This equation can be written as P​(x,mp​(x))=pP(x,m_{p}(x))=p, where PP is a normalized incomplete gamma function. See [5, 8.2.4]. The asymptotic behaviour at infinity of the quantiles in the gamma distribution was investigated in the papers [7] and [4] (and for the beta distribution in [8]). We complement this by an investigation at the origin and revisit the expansion at infinity via an elementary method, inspired by [2]. Notice that the main focus in [2] (and [3]) was on monotonicity properties of the median m=m1/2m=m_{1/2}, and the so-called Chen-Rubin conjecture.

The behaviour of mm and m′m^{\prime} at the origin was in [2] shown to be

m⁡(x)∼e−γ​e−log⁡2x,m′​(x)∼log⁡2x2​e−γ​e−log⁡2xas​x→0.m(x)\sim e^{-\gamma}e^{-\frac{\log 2}{x}},\quad m^{\prime}(x)\sim\frac{\log 2}{x^{2}}e^{-\gamma}e^{-\frac{\log 2}{x}}\quad\text{as}\ x\to 0.

Introducing the function u⁡(x)=elog⁡2/x​m​(x)u(x)=e^{\nicefrac{{\log 2}}{{x}}}m(x) it thus follows that u⁡(x)→e−γu(x)\to e^{-\gamma} for x→0x\to 0. A plot of the function uu leaves the impression that also its derivative has a finite and positive limit at zero. See Figure 1. Let us mention that the asymptotic behaviour of mm and m′m^{\prime} at the origin as displayed above is not sufficient for determining the behaviour of u′u^{\prime}. In fact, these relations only yield that

x2​u′​(x)=x2​elog⁡2x​m′​(x)−(log⁡2)​elog⁡2x​m​(x)x^{2}u^{\prime}(x)=x^{2}e^{\frac{\log 2}{x}}m^{\prime}(x)-(\log 2)e^{\frac{\log 2}{x}}m(x)

tends to zero as xx tends to zero.

We define, for p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and x>0x>0,

up​(x)=e−log⁡px​mp​(x).u_{p}(x)=e^{-\frac{\log p}{x}}m_{p}(x). (2)

Experimenting with plots of these functions (for different pp) indicate that their behaviour at the origin do not depend on pp. This motivates the results of the paper in which the asymptotic behaviour of upu_{p} at the origin is studied.

In Proposition 2.4 it is shown that up∈C∞​([0,∞))u_{p}\in C^{\infty}([0,\infty)) and that any derivative of upu_{p} at the origin can be computed explicitly, and does not depend on pp. (It follows from the implicit function theorem that mpm_{p} and hence also upu_{p} are C∞C^{\infty}-functions on (0,∞)(0,\infty).) In Proposition 3.2 and Corallary 3.3 the asymptotic behaviour of upu_{p} is used to obtain the asymptotic behaviour of mpm_{p} and its derivatives at the origin. In particular it is proved that for any n≥0n\geq 0,

mp(n)​(x)∼(−log⁡p)nx2​n​e−γ​elog⁡pxas​x→0,m_{p}^{(n)}(x)\sim\frac{(-\log p)^{n}}{x^{2n}}e^{-\gamma}e^{\frac{\log p}{x}}\quad\text{as}\ x\to 0,

generalizing the two relations mentioned above. See [1] for the asymptotic behaviour at zero of the quantiles in the beta distribution as a function of one of the parameters.

In Appendix A some remarks on the asymptotic behaviour of mpm_{p} at infinity are given. Another procedure (compared to [7] and [4]) is described and Maple code is given. We stress that our result, Theorem A.6, is also given in [4].

Let us end the introduction with a basic result about the quantiles.

Lemma 1.1.

The function mpm_{p} is strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Furthermore, limx→0mp​(x)=0\lim_{x\to 0}m_{p}(x)=0 and limx→∞mp​(x)=∞\lim_{x\to\infty}m_{p}(x)=\infty.

Proof.

The family {e−t​tx−1​d​t/Γ⁡(x)}x>0\{e^{-t}t^{x-1}dt/\Gamma(x)\}_{x>0} is a convolution semigroup of probabilities on [0,∞)[0,\infty) and the assertions in the lemma hold for any convolution semigroup of probabilities on [0,∞)[0,\infty). This is proved in the same way as [2, Proposition 2.1], replacing 1/2\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} by pp. ∎

The limit of upu_{p} (defined in (2)) at zero is given in Proposition 2.2 and depends on the next lemma.

Lemma 2.1.

We have limx→0mp​(x)x=p\lim_{x\to 0}m_{p}(x)^{x}=p.

Proof.

mp​(x)x​e−mp​(x)\displaystyle m_{p}(x)^{x}e^{-m_{p}(x)} =x​∫0mp​(x)tx−1​e−t​𝑑t−∫0mp​(x)tx​e−t​𝑑t\displaystyle=x\int_{0}^{m_{p}(x)}t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt-\int_{0}^{m_{p}(x)}t^{x}e^{-t}\,dt
=p​Γ​(x+1)−∫0mp​(x)tx​e−t​𝑑t,\displaystyle=p\Gamma(x+1)-\int_{0}^{m_{p}(x)}t^{x}e^{-t}\,dt, (3)

and since mp​(x)→0m_{p}(x)\to 0 for x→0x\to 0 the proof is complete. ∎

where ℓp​(x)=x​log⁡mp​(x)\ell_{p}(x)=x\log m_{p}(x). From Lemma 1.1 and Lemma 2.1 it follows that limx→0ℓp′​(x)=Γ′​(1)=−γ\lim_{x\to 0}\ell_{p}^{\prime}(x)=\Gamma^{\prime}(1)=-\gamma. Applying l’Hospital’s rule we obtain

limx→0log⁡up​(x)=limx→0ℓp​(x)−log⁡px=limx→0ℓp′​(x)=−γ\lim_{x\to 0}\log u_{p}(x)=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\ell_{p}(x)-\log p}{x}=\lim_{x\to 0}\ell_{p}^{\prime}(x)=-\gamma

and this completes the proof.∎

By differentiation of the relation (4) one obtains an involved expression containing only one term with up′′​(x)u_{p}^{\prime\prime}(x). It turns out that it is possible to compute the limit up′′​(0)u_{p}^{\prime\prime}(0) and express it in terms of up′​(0)u_{p}^{\prime}(0) and up​(0)u_{p}(0). The next step is to show that any derivative up(n)​(x)u_{p}^{(n)}(x) has a limit as xx tends to 00, and hence that up∈C∞​([0,∞))u_{p}\in C^{\infty}([0,\infty)).

Proposition 2.4.

The limit

limx→0up(n)​(x)\lim_{x\to 0}u_{p}^{(n)}(x)

exists for any n≥0n\geq 0 and is independent of pp.

The proof of this proposition is carried out by an inductive argument. In order to do so some computational lemmas are needed. We shall also use the notation ∂xj\partial_{x}^{j} to denote the jjth derivative when it is convenient. As one would expect, the function

αp​(x)=elog⁡px\alpha_{p}(x)=e^{\frac{\log p}{x}} (5)

plays a key role in the development. Its behaviour is determined by the following lemma.

Lemma 2.5.

For any n≥1n\geq 1,

∂xn(e−1/x)=pn(1/x)e−1/x,\partial_{x}^{n}\left(e^{-1/x}\right)=p_{n}(1/x)e^{-1/x},

where pn​(t)=∑k=n+12​nak,n​tkp_{n}(t)=\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n}a_{k,n}t^{k} with ak,n∈ℤa_{k,n}\in\mathbb{Z}. Furthermore a2​n,n=1a_{2n,n}=1, a2​n−1,n=−n⁡(n−1)a_{2n-1,n}=-n(n-1) and a2​n−2,n=n​(n−1)2​(n−2)/2a_{2n-2,n}=n(n-1)^{2}(n-2)/2.

Proof.

This is a standard induction argument, and the sequence {pn}\{p_{n}\} is easily shown to satisfy pn+1​(t)=t2​(pn​(t)−pn′​(t))p_{n+1}(t)=t^{2}(p_{n}(t)-p_{n}^{\prime}(t)). ∎

Lemma 2.6.

Suppose that the limit limx→0up(j)​(x)\lim_{x\to 0}u_{p}^{(j)}(x) exists in ℝ\mathbb{R} for j=0,…,qj=0,\ldots,q. Then limx→0mp(j)​(x)=0\lim_{x\to 0}m_{p}^{(j)}(x)=0 for j=0,…,qj=0,\ldots,q.

Proof.

This follows from the relation (with αp\alpha_{p} as in (5))

mp(j)​(x)=∑l=0j(jl)​αp(l)​(x)​up(j−l)​(x),m_{p}^{(j)}(x)=\sum_{l=0}^{j}\binom{j}{l}\alpha_{p}^{(l)}(x)u_{p}^{(j-l)}(x),

combined with the fact that αp(l)​(x)→0\alpha_{p}^{(l)}(x)\to 0 for x→0x\to 0 for all l≥0l\geq 0. ∎

I1​(x)=up​(x)x+1​(1x+1+∑k=1∞(−1)kk!​mp​(x)kx+k+1).I_{1}(x)=u_{p}(x)^{x+1}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}\frac{m_{p}(x)^{k}}{x+k+1}\right).

Using the Taylor series expansion of the exponential function we get

which gives the desired formula. ∎

I2​(x)\displaystyle I_{2}(x) =up​(x)x​log⁡up​(x)​∑k=0∞(−1)k(k+1)!​mp​(x)k+1x+k+1\displaystyle=u_{p}(x)^{x}\log u_{p}(x)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{(k+1)!}\frac{m_{p}(x)^{k+1}}{x+k+1}

This follows the same lines as the proof of Lemma 2.7, noticing that

∫0up​(x)sx+k​log⁡s​𝑑s=up​(x)x+k+1x+k+1​log⁡up​(x)−up​(x)x+k+1(x+k+1)2.\int_{0}^{u_{p}(x)}s^{x+k}\log s\,ds=\frac{u_{p}(x)^{x+k+1}}{x+k+1}\log u_{p}(x)-\frac{u_{p}(x)^{x+k+1}}{(x+k+1)^{2}}.

∎

Lemma 2.9.

Suppose that limx→0up(j)​(x)\lim_{x\to 0}u_{p}^{(j)}(x) exists in ℝ\mathbb{R} for j=0,…,qj=0,\ldots,q. Then

limx→0∂xjI1​(x)\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\partial_{x}^{j}I_{1}(x) =limx→0∂xj(up​(x)x+1x+1),and\displaystyle=\lim_{x\to 0}\partial_{x}^{j}\left(\frac{u_{p}(x)^{x+1}}{x+1}\right),\ \text{and}

for j=0,…,qj=0,\ldots,q.

Proof.

This follows from Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 2.8, noticing that termwise differentiation is permitted and that the limit of any term involving mp​(x)m_{p}(x) in a positive power equals zero. ∎

Appendix A Asymptotic behaviour at infinity; Maple code

The purpose of this appendix is to outline a method where the asymptotic behaviour of the function

φp​(x)=log⁡(xmp​(x))\varphi_{p}(x)=\log\left(\frac{x}{m_{p}(x)}\right)

is used to find the asymptotic behaviour of mpm_{p}. Our method is quite elementary, basically only Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem is used. The notation

f⁡(x)∼∑k=0∞βkxk,x→∞f(x)\sim\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\beta_{k}}{x^{k}},\quad x\to\infty

means that for any NN, f⁡(x)−∑k=0Nβk/xk=O⁡(x−N−1)f(x)-\sum_{k=0}^{N}\beta_{k}/x^{k}=O(x^{-N-1}) as x→∞x\to\infty. Inserting Euler’s integral representation of Γ⁡(x)\Gamma(x) in (1), changing variables to u=log⁡(x/t)u=\log(x/t) and performing some manipulations we obtain

∫0φp​(x)e−x⁡(e−u+u)​𝑑u\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\varphi_{p}(x)}e^{-x(e^{-u}+u)}\,du =(1−p)​∫0∞e−x⁡(e−u+u)​𝑑u−p​∫0∞e−x⁡(eu−u)​𝑑u.\displaystyle=(1-p)\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x(e^{-u}+u)}\,du-p\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x(e^{u}-u)}\,du. (9)

By multiplication by exe^{x} and the change of variable s=x​us=\sqrt{x}u we get

∫0x​φp​(x)e−s2​h​(−s/x)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x)}e^{-s^{2}h(-\nicefrac{{s}}{{\sqrt{x}}})}\,ds =(1−p)​J1​(x)−p​J2​(x),\displaystyle=(1-p)J_{1}(x)-pJ_{2}(x), (10)

where hh is the positive and increasing function on ℝ\mathbb{R} defined as

h⁡(u)=eu−1−uu2=∑k=0∞1(k+2)!​uk,h(u)=\frac{e^{u}-1-u}{u^{2}}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(k+2)!}u^{k}, (11)

and

J1​(x)=∫0∞e−s2​h​(−s/x)​𝑑s,J2​(x)=∫0∞e−s2​h​(s/x)​𝑑s.J_{1}(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-s^{2}h(-\nicefrac{{s}}{{\sqrt{x}}})}\,ds,\quad J_{2}(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-s^{2}h(\nicefrac{{s}}{{\sqrt{x}}})}\,ds.

A fundamental sequence of polynomials is introduced in the next lemma (which is proved by induction).

Let n≥0n\geq 0. There exists a polynomial QnQ_{n} of n+1n+1 variables such that

+∑k=1N+1Akxk/2+o(1x(N+1)/2),\displaystyle\phantom{=}+\sum_{k=1}^{N+1}\frac{A_{k}}{x^{k/2}}+o\left(\frac{1}{x^{(N+1)/2}}\right),

since (x​φp​(x)−Lp)j+1/xk/2=o⁡(1/x(N+1)/2)\left(\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x)-L_{p}\right)^{j+1}/x^{k/2}=o(1/x^{(N+1)/2}) for j+k≥N+1j+k\geq N+1 and this shows that x​φp​(x)−Lp\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x)-L_{p} has an asymptotic expansion up to order (N+1)/2(N+1)/2. k+j≥1,j+1≤l≤N+j,k+l=N+1.k+j\geq 1,\quad j+1\leq l\leq N+j,\quad k+l=N+1.

Then

aN+1=1q0​(Lp)​(∑(k,l,j)∈TN(−1)k+1​qk(j)​(Lp)k!​(j+1)!​aj,l+AN+1).\displaystyle a_{N+1}=\frac{1}{q_{0}(L_{p})}\left(\sum_{(k,l,j)\in T_{N}}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}q_{k}^{(j)}(L_{p})}{k!(j+1)!}a_{j,l}+A_{N+1}\right). (20)

Remark A.5.

It is evident that also J1′J_{1}^{\prime} and J2′J_{2}^{\prime} have asymptotic expansions at infinity. From the relation

(x​φp​(x))′​e−(x​φp​(x))2​h​(CLOSE\displaystyle(\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x))^{\prime}e^{-(\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x))^{2}}h( −xφp(x)/x)=(1−p)J1′(x)−pJ2′(x)\displaystyle-\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x)/\sqrt{x})=(1-p)J_{1}^{\prime}(x)-pJ_{2}^{\prime}(x)
+∫0x​φp​(x)e−22h(−s/x)h′(−s/x)s3ds12​x3/2\displaystyle\phantom{=}+\int_{0}^{\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x)}e^{-2^{2}h(-s/\sqrt{x})}h^{\prime}(-s/\sqrt{x})s^{3}\,ds\frac{1}{2x^{3/2}}

it follows that also (x​φp​(x))′(\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x))^{\prime} has an asymptotic expansion at infinity.

Theorem A.6.

The pp-quantile mpm_{p} has an asymptotic expansion at infinity:

mp​(x)∼∑n=−2∞τnxn/2=x−Lp​x1/2+(Lp2−1)/3+(Lp​(7−Lp2)/36)​x−1/2+….m_{p}(x)\sim\sum_{n=-2}^{\infty}\frac{\tau_{n}}{x^{n/2}}=x-L_{p}\,x^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}}+\nicefrac{{(L_{p}^{2}-1)}}{{3}}+(\nicefrac{{L_{p}(7-L_{p}^{2})}}{{36}})\,x^{-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}}+\ldots.
Proof.

This follows from Lemma A.4 and the relation mp​(x)=x​e−φp​(x)m_{p}(x)=xe^{-\varphi_{p}(x)}. ∎

This result was obtained in [4, Theorem 1.3], where it was also obtained that the coefficient τn\tau_{n} is a polynomial of degree n+2n+2 with rational coefficients independent of pp, evaluated at LpL_{p}. It is an even (resp. odd) polynomial when nn is even (resp. odd). These facts, except the degree being n+2n+2, can also be obtained via the method outlined above but we skip the details.

Maple code for computing the polynomials in the expansions of φp\varphi_{p} and mpm_{p} is given below. We get (in accordance with [4, Table 2] since L1−p=−LpL_{1-p}=-L_{p})

τ2​(t)\displaystyle\tau_{2}(t) =−t4/270−t2/810+8/405\displaystyle=-\nicefrac{{t^{4}}}{{270}}-\nicefrac{{t^{2}}}{{810}}+\nicefrac{{8}}{{405}}
τ3​(t)\displaystyle\tau_{3}(t) =−t5/4320−8​t3/1215+433​t/38880\displaystyle=-\nicefrac{{t^{5}}}{{4320}}-\nicefrac{{8t^{3}}}{{1215}}+\nicefrac{{433t}}{{38880}}
τ4​(t)\displaystyle\tau_{4}(t) =t6/17010−t4/840−923​t2/204120+184/25515\displaystyle=\nicefrac{{t^{6}}}{{17010}}-\nicefrac{{t^{4}}}{{840}}-\nicefrac{{923t^{2}}}{{204120}}+\nicefrac{{184}}{{25515}}
τ5​(t)\displaystyle\tau_{5}(t) =139​t7/5443200+1451​t5/48988800−289517​t3/146966400−289717​t/146966400.\displaystyle=\nicefrac{{139t^{7}}}{{5443200}}+\nicefrac{{1451t^{5}}}{{48988800}}-\nicefrac{{289517t^{3}}}{{146966400}}-\nicefrac{{289717t}}{{146966400}}.

The procedure Qpol computes the polynomial Qk​(s)Q_{k}(s) defined in (12):

Qpol := proc(k, s)
    local T, l, h;
    h := v -> (exp(v) - v - 1)/v^2;
    T := 1;
    for l to k do
       T := diff(T, v) - s^2*T*diff(h(v), v);
    end do;
    limit(T, v = 0);
end proc;

The procedure qkj computes qk(j)​(L)q_{k}^{(j)}(L) from the proof of Lemma A.4 at LL:

qkj := proc(j, k)
    local T;
    if j = 0 then
       T := s^k*Qpol(k, s)*exp(-1/2*s^2);
    else
       T := diff(s^k*Qpol(k, s)*exp(-1/2*s^2), s $ j);
    end if;
    eval(T, s = L);
end proc;

The procedure compute(j,n) computes the coefficient aj,na_{j,n} of x−n/2x^{-n/2} in the asymptotic expansion of (x​φp​(x)−Lp)j+1\left(\sqrt{x}\varphi_{p}(x)-L_{p}\right)^{j+1}.

compute := proc(j, n)
    local T, q;
    global a;
    T := 0;
    if j = 0 then
       T := a[0, n - j];
    else for q from 0 to n - j - 1 do
            T := T + a[j - 1, q + j]*a[0, n - j - q];
         end do;
    end if;
    T;
end proc;

The numbers AkA_{k} can be computed using the functions

c := k -> int(s^k*Qpol(k, s)*exp(-1/2*s^2), s = 0 .. infinity);
d := k -> int(s^k*Qpol(k, s)*exp(-1/2*s^2), s = 0 .. L);
A := k -> ((1 - p)*(-1)^k*c(k) - p*c(k) - (-1)^k*d(k))/k!;

For a given MM, the coefficients a0,a1,…,aM+1a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{M+1} are computed using (20):

M := 7;
for j from 0 to M do
    for l from 0 to M do a[j, l] := 0; end do;
end do;
a[0, 1] := (1 + L^2/2)/3;
for N from 1 to M do
    S := 0;
    for k from 0 to N do
        l := N + 1 - k;
        for j from max(0, 1 - k) to l - 1 do
            a[j,l] := compute(j,l);
            S := S + (-1)^(k+1)*qkj(j, k)*a[j,l]/(k!*(j+1)!);
        end do;
    end do;
    S := S + A(N + 1);
    p := 1/2 - erf(L/sqrt(2))/2;
    a[0, N + 1] := simplify(S*exp(L^2/2));
end do

for l from 0 to M + 1 do
    print(eval(a[0, l]));
end do

Finally the expansion of mpm_{p} is found using mp​(x)=x​e−ϕp​(x)m_{p}(x)=xe^{-\phi_{p}(x)}. We found it convenient to change variable to y=1/xy=1/\sqrt{x} and use taylor:

phip_of_y := L*y + sum(a[0, l]*y^(l + 1), l = 0 .. M);
temp := convert(taylor(exp(-phip_of_y), y = 0, M + 1), polynom);
collect(expand(x*eval(temp, y = 1/x^(1/2))), x);
